name: Trae Stephens
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Forbes' own profile page names him and states "Trae Stephens is ranked at No. 7 on the 2026 Midas List, his 3rd appearance" (https://www.forbes.com/profile/trae-stephens/), and describes him as General Partner at Founders Fund and Executive Chairman of Anduril. a1: born November 1983 (Wikipedia short description and lead; Forbes gives age 42, consistent). a2: Georgetown University School of Foreign Service, degree in Regional and Comparative Studies (Middle East), 2005 -- Wikipedia states he "earned a degree in Regional and Comparative Studies (Middle East) in 2005". SECOND ATTEMPT MADE: Founders Fund's own team page (foundersfund.com/team/trae-stephens/) confirms the School of Foreign Service but gives no year, and the Generalist's long-form Founders Fund profile confirms Georgetown and a Middle Eastern Studies major but gives no year either. No graduate degree found in any source. Confidence medium because only one source carries the year, though three carry the institution and field. a3: first job in the INVESTING domain is Founders Fund, March 2013 -- Wikipedia: "Stephens began to work for the Founders Fund in 2013"; the Generalist's profile independently states he joined in March 2013 after a Thanksgiving offer from Thiel. His earlier career (US Intelligence Community computational linguist from 2005, Palantir from 2008) is operating work, not finance, so it does not set a3 -- same convention as p151 Mignot and p06 Meeker, where a3 is the first FINANCE-domain job. a4: co-founded Anduril Industries in 2017 with Palmer Luckey (Wikipedia). SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture found. Anduril (2017) is his first company; Varda Space Industries (2020), Sol/Sindarin (2021) and Valinor Enterprises (2024) all come later. This does not move the hit in any case, because the investors_finance criterion for a fund manager is fund100, not rev10. EARLIER-FIRM CHECK (the assignment's specific instruction): Stephens was never a named GP at an earlier FIRM. Before Founders Fund he was an operator -- an early Palantir employee, 2008-2013 -- not an investor, so there is no earlier fund vehicle to test. FUND100 -- FUND PROGRESSION FROM SEC EDGAR FORM D RELATED-PERSONS LISTS (curl with a research User-Agent; efts.sec.gov full-text search for "Trae Stephens" across all forms). The Form D related-persons block is the document that NAMES the general partners of a specific fund vehicle, which is exactly what frame.md's fund100 wording requires, and it is the same evidence used for p130 Green, p131 Miura-Ko and p151 Mignot. Founders Fund V, LP (CIK 1601419, Form D 2014-03-06, $1,015,200,000 sold): managing members of the GP are Thiel, Howery, Nosek, Singerman -- NOT Stephens. Founders Fund VI, LP (CIK 1669874, Form D 2016-03-25): same four -- NOT Stephens. Founders Fund VII, LP (CIK 1792034, Form D 2019-11-20, $1,496,368,333): Thiel, Singerman, Rabois -- NOT Stephens. Founders Fund VIII, LP (CIK 1912108, Form D 2022-03-04, $1,927,770,000): Thiel, Singerman, Rabois -- NOT Stephens. Founders Fund IX, LP (CIK 1971631): the FIRST vehicle naming him. The original Form D, filed 2023-04-04, lists "Trae Stephens ... Managing Member of the General Partner of the Issuer" alongside Thiel, Singerman, Rabois and Napoleon Ta, with totalOfferingAmount $675,000,000. The 2025-10-16 Form D/A for the same fund gives dateOfFirstSale 2023-04-07 and totalAmountSold $971,584,000, again naming Stephens as a managing member of the GP. EDGAR full-text search returns no earlier filing of any kind naming him as a fund GP; his other named-GP vehicles (Founders Fund Growth III, 2025; Growth IV, 2026) are later. FIGURE VS THAT YEAR'S BAR: the 2023 fund100 bar is $94,644,704 nominal (python -m src.cpi 2023). Even the initial $675,000,000 offering is 713% of the bar, and the $971,584,000 finally sold is 1,027%. Margin is enormous; nothing near the 20% caution band. JUDGMENT CALL TO FLAG: Founders Fund's own team page titles him "Partner" and Wikipedia says "In 2014, he became a partner at Founders Fund", while Forbes' 2026 profile titles him "General Partner". A firm-internal "partner" title is not the same thing as being a named general partner OF A FUND, and the SEC record is unambiguous that he was not one on Funds V through VIII. So the anchor is 2023, not 2014. This is a nine-year gap and is the one place this row could be argued; it is recorded on the documentary reading of frame.md's word "named". a6: Anduril, the thing he is famous for now, reached the scale it is known for by 2025 -- Wikipedia: "In June 2025, Stephens became a billionaire after Anduril's Series G fundraising round"; Forbes adds that Anduril "was last valued at $61 billion in May 2026". Best-effort, medium confidence.

name: Billie Eilish
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: grammy.com's own 68th Annual Grammy Awards results page returns HTTP 200 to curl with a browser User-Agent and carries the entry "WILDFLOWER / Billie Eilish, Finneas O'Connell" with credits "Billie Eilish O'Connell & Finneas O'Connell, songwriters (Billie Eilish)" under Song Of The Year (https://www.grammy.com/awards/68th-annual-grammy-awards-2025/). Wikipedia independently records ten Grammy wins. a1: born Billie Eilish Pirate Baird O'Connell in Los Angeles on 18 December 2001 (Wikipedia, citing Billboard). a2: UNKNOWN AFTER FOUR GENUINE ATTEMPTS -- this is the one anchor that could not be sourced. Eilish was homeschooled by her mother Maggie Baird throughout and told Reason in January 2020 "I've never been to school. I grew up homeschooled, stayed homeschooled, never was not homeschooled" (https://reason.com/2020/01/28/sibling-grammy-winners-billie-eilish-and-finneas-oconnell-praise-homeschooling/), which explicitly rules out a school-leaving date. Attempts made: (1) the full Wikipedia article, which describes the homeschooling but gives no completion, diploma or exam; (2) the Reason piece above, which the fetch confirms says nothing about an equivalency exam, diploma or graduation; (3) two web searches for a graduation/equivalency year, which returned only content-farm pages (celebanswers.com, cercorlearning.com, skillnation.in, educationnext.in) repeating an identical uncredited sentence that she "passed her equivalency exam and graduated high school when she was only 15" -- no primary or reputable outlet carries it, and at age 15 the window spans Dec 2016 to Dec 2017 in any case; (4) the Vogue March 2020 cover story, which Wikipedia cites for the homeschooling, is not fetchable from this environment. Recording unknown rather than dating the row off recycled aggregator copy. a3: 2016 -- in January 2016 Finneas and his manager Danny Rukasin arranged a deal in which Apple Music signed Eilish to the A&R company Platoon, her first professional/commercial engagement in the music domain (Wikipedia). This follows the p153 Bad Bunny convention, where a3 is the year of the first professional signing rather than childhood performance; her earlier Los Angeles Children's Chorus membership at age eight was unpaid participation, not a job. Confidence medium because only the month/year of the deal, not a start date, is given. a4: 18 November 2015 -- "Ocean Eyes" uploaded to SoundCloud, her first independently released own work (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Eyes_(song); the archived SoundCloud object's own metadata gives created_at 2015-11-19T03:18:57Z, i.e. the evening of 18 November 2015 US Pacific time). SERIAL/EARLIER-WORK CHECK: no earlier released work found. Wikipedia's early-life section records only a first song written at age 11 for her mother's songwriting class, never released. "Ocean Eyes" is the first public release. AUD1M -- CROSSING PINNED TO WITHIN FIVE DAYS FROM ARCHIVED PRIMARY COUNTERS. The audience bar is a flat 1,000,000 headcount, so no CPI adjustment applies. The SoundCloud track page for "Ocean Eyes" embeds SoundCloud's own playback_count in the page JSON, and the Internet Archive holds near-daily snapshots. Reading playback_count straight out of the archived pages (web.archive.org id_ raw captures of https://soundcloud.com/billieeilish/ocean-eyes): 2016-08-12 = 597,446; 2016-12-01 = 957,113; 2016-12-10 = 995,173; 2016-12-15 = 1,016,670; 2016-12-19 = 1,034,308; 2016-12-25 = 1,058,171; 2016-12-31 = 1,082,656; 2017-01-01 = 1,085,951; 2017-03-01 = 1,383,168. The 1,000,000 line was therefore crossed between 10 and 15 December 2016 -- unambiguously inside calendar 2016, with no inference and no interpolation needed. That is on SoundCloud ALONE; the official "Ocean Eyes" music video had been on YouTube since 24 March 2016 and Darkroom/Interscope re-released the track for download and streaming on 18 November 2016, so total audience across platforms crossed 1M no later than this and probably earlier. Using the single-platform counter makes 2016 a conservative, fully sourced date rather than a bounded one. MARGIN WATCH -- UNDER 20%: the first archived above-bar reading, 1,016,670 on 2016-12-15, is only 101.7% of the 1,000,000 bar. The thinness is inherent to pinning a crossing rather than a scale level: the counter is an exact integer either side of an exact threshold (995,173 below on 10 Dec, 1,016,670 above on 15 Dec), so there is no measurement uncertainty to eat the margin, and by 1 March 2017 the same counter reads 138% of the bar. Flagged as instructed nonetheless. OWN-WORK BOUNDARY: "Ocean Eyes" was written, mixed and produced by her brother Finneas, with Eilish as the performing artist and the credited recording artist. Treated as her own work under the p34 N'Dour and p53 Tems precedent, which count a co-credited or featured recording as the artist's own for aud1m. a6: 2019 -- her debut studio album When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go? (29 March 2019) "debuted atop the US Billboard 200 and UK Albums Chart and was one of the year's best-selling albums" (Wikipedia), the point at which the global-pop-star status she is known for now was established; the Grammy Big Four sweep followed in January 2020. Best-effort, medium confidence.

name: Bess Wohl
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: pulitzer.org (curl, browser User-Agent; WebFetch is 403'd) 2026 winners page, Drama block: "Liberation, by Bess Wohl -- A striking blend of comedy and sincerity that explores the legacy of the consciousness-raising feminist groups of the 1970s, using the story of the playwright's mother..." (https://www.pulitzer.org/prize-winners-by-year/2026). The Internet Broadway Database independently records "Pulitzer Prize for Drama 2026 | Winner | Liberation, Written by Bess Wohl" (https://www.ibdb.com/broadway-cast-staff/bess-wohl-500779). a1: UNKNOWN AFTER THREE ATTEMPTS. English Wikipedia carries no birth date and files her under Category:Year of birth missing (living people). Wikidata (Q-item for Bess Wohl) does assert 1975, but its ONLY reference is "imported from Italian Wikipedia" -- a circular Wikipedia-to-Wikipedia import with no underlying source, which does not meet this study's sourcing bar. The Library of Congress name authority file, which usually carries birth years for published dramatists, lists eight Bess Wohl playtexts (Dramatists Play Service, Faber, Broadway Licensing, Overlook) under the heading "Wohl, Bess" with NO date qualifier at all. IBDB gives gender only. Recorded unknown rather than laundering the Wikidata year. a2: UNKNOWN AFTER FIVE ATTEMPTS -- flagged, since a2 is the study's binding constraint. Sources agree on the credentials but none gives a year: Wikipedia's infobox says Harvard University (BA) and Yale University (MFA), and the body adds "She went to Harvard College for an BA in English, and then went to the Yale School of Drama for an MFA in acting", with no dates. Attempts that produced no year: Faber's author page for her (faber.co.uk), Concord Theatricals / Dramatists Play Service author lookup, the Roundabout Theatre Liberation programme site, IBDB, and a Harvard Crimson site search (returns no matching articles). A dating route via her student play Cats Talk Back -- created at Yale and later winner of Best Overall Production at the New York International Fringe Festival -- was attempted and failed: no source found dates that Fringe production either. WebSearch was unavailable for this row (shared 200-call budget exhausted), which removed the usual route to a dated interview or profile. a3: 2004 -- her first professional theatre credit is as an ACTRESS, playing Alegra in Chinese Friends Off-Broadway at Playwrights Horizons, per the credits table in her Wikipedia article. Following the p05 Bong Joon-ho convention (a3 = first job in the craft's industry even when the role differs from the one they became known for), acting Off-Broadway counts as the theatre domain. Medium confidence: an adversarial reading that the relevant domain is playwriting specifically would move a3 to 2012 or 2014. a4: 2012 -- Barcelona, her first datable produced play, premiered at the Contemporary American Theater Festival (Wikipedia). MEDIUM, AND FLAGGED: her genuinely first independently created work is Cats Talk Back, written while she was a Yale student and taken to the New York International Fringe Festival, but no source found dates it, so the true a4 is earlier than 2012 by an unknown margin. AUD1M -- EXCLUDED, crossing_undatable. The bar is a flat 1,000,000 headcount; no CPI adjustment applies. Every candidate work was checked and none produces a dated 1M audience: (1) THEATRE, the roster's expected path. Her two Broadway runs are the largest single audiences available and both fall two orders of magnitude short: IBDB gives Grand Horizons at the Hayes Theater (a 597-seat house) from 23 January to 1 March 2020, and Liberation at the James Earl Jones Theatre (about 1,079 seats) from 28 October 2025 to 1 February 2026 -- on the order of 10^5 seats sold at absolute most across both. The Off-Broadway runs (American Hero and Pretty Filthy 2015, Small Mouth Sounds at Ars Nova 2015 and Signature 2016, Continuity and Make Believe 2019, Liberation at the Laura Pels 2025), the 2017 Small Mouth Sounds US national tour, and the West End runs of Camp Siegfried (Old Vic 2021) and Barcelona (Duke of York's 2024) are all smaller still. A CUMULATIVE million across a decade of licensed productions is conceivable but no source counts it and no source dates it -- which is precisely the crossing_undatable condition, and matches the roster note's own warning that in theatre a million-person audience "accumulates across productions rather than landing at once". (2) SCREEN. Her one film as writer-director, Baby Ruby (world premiere TIFF 9 September 2022, US release 3 February 2023, Magnet Releasing), grossed $16,991 worldwide per Box Office Mojo and The Numbers, both cited in its Wikipedia infobox -- roughly a four-figure theatrical audience. No streaming viewership figure exists for it. No other screenwriting credit of hers could be found: neither Wikipedia's article nor its 'what links here' index (checked via the API) surfaces any film or television series she wrote, despite 'screenwriter' appearing in her occupation list. Her acting credits are other people's work and would not count as her own under aud1m in any case. PER THE CALIBRATION NOTE IN THE BRIEF: this is an honest exclusion, not a failure to look. Dating this row off the 2026 Pulitzer would be exactly the defect frame.md forbids -- the prize is the membership vehicle, not the hit. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: not applicable (non-commercial bucket, no ventures). a6: 2026 -- Liberation won both the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Play in 2026 (pulitzer.org 2026 winners page; IBDB awards table), the point at which the reputation she now has was established.

name: Jill Lepore
hit_entity: The New Yorker essays (from "People Power", 24 October 2005)
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: pulitzer.org returns HTTP 200 to curl with a browser User-Agent (WebFetch is 403'd), and the 2026 winners page's History block reads "We the People: A History of the U.S. Constitution, by Jill Lepore (Liveright) -- A lively and engaging narrative that investigates why the Constitution is so difficult to amend..." (https://www.pulitzer.org/prize-winners-by-year/2026). Prize organisation's own citation, naming the person. a1: born 27 August 1966, West Boylston, Massachusetts (Wikipedia infobox). a2: PhD, American Studies, Yale University, 1995 -- HER OWN SITE is the pinning source: "Lepore received a B.A. in English from Tufts University in 1987, an M.A. in American Culture from the University of Michigan in 1990, and a Ph.D. in American Studies from Yale University in 1995" (https://jilllepore.com/about). This second source was sought deliberately because Wikipedia carries a {{fails verification}} tag on exactly that sentence; her own bio resolves it and confirms all three degrees and years, so confidence is high. a3: 1995 -- "Lepore taught at the University of California, San Diego from 1995 to 1996 and at Boston University beginning in 1996; she started at Harvard in 2003" (Wikipedia). Her craft IS history, so a history teaching post is in-domain, unlike the p33 Morrison case where literature teaching was ruled adjacent to the authorship domain. Confidence medium: only Wikipedia carries the UCSD years; her own bio starts at Harvard 2003. a4: 1998 -- The Name of War, her first book (Knopf), which won the Bancroft Prize (Wikipedia; jilllepore.com). SERIAL/EARLIER-WORK CHECK: no earlier independently created work found. The Wikipedia bibliography's articles section opens with a single June 2001 Journal of American History essay; nothing of hers precedes the 1998 book except academic journal work. AUD1M -- BOUNDED 2005-2006, ONE-YEAR SPAN, BOTH ENDS SOURCED. The bar is a flat 1,000,000 headcount; no CPI adjustment applies. UPPER END: the Magazine Publishers of America table "Top 100 ABC magazines by average circulation First Half 2006", captured by the Internet Archive on 2 December 2006, lists NEW YORKER at rank 85 with subscriptions 1,018,337, single-copy sales 43,973, total average circulation 1,062,310 -- an Audit Bureau of Circulations audited third-party figure. Lepore published four New Yorker essays inside that audit window and its immediate aftermath ("Plymouth Rocked", 24 April 2006; "Goodbye, Columbus", 8 May 2006; "Westward Ho!", 9 October 2006; "The Sharpened Quill", 16 October 2006), so an above-1M audience for her own work is documented for 2006. LOWER END: the founding-year analogue from frame.md -- an audience cannot precede the work. Wikipedia's Jill Lepore bibliography dates her FIRST New Yorker piece to "People power", Books, 24 October 2005, vol. 81 issue 33, pp. 80-84 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Lepore_bibliography), and Wikipedia's article text agrees she "has contributed since 2005". Nothing of hers before that could have carried a 1M audience: her prior output is one Journal of American History essay (2001) and three university-press/Knopf history books, none with any sourced sales figure remotely near 1M. The crossing is therefore between her first New Yorker issue (October 2005) and the audited 2006 circulation. It is very likely 2005 itself -- the October 2005 issue's circulation would have been within a percent or two of the H1 2006 figure -- but no 2005 audit figure could be sourced (two attempts: the Wayback CDX index holds no earlier MPA/ABC circulation table, and WebSearch was unavailable, see below), so the row is bounded rather than pinned. MARGIN WATCH -- UNDER 20%: 1,062,310 total circulation is 106.2% of the 1,000,000 bar, and the subscription component alone (1,018,337) is 101.8%. Both are inside the 20% caution band and are flagged. Two things push the true figure well clear: circulation counts copies, not readers, and pass-along readership for a weekly is a multiple of circulation (Wikipedia's Readership section cites MediaMark Research audience surveys rather than circulation for exactly this reason); and the figure rose steadily thereafter -- The New Yorker's own October 2025 Statement of Ownership gives total circulation 1,319,919. But the CROSSING is what is being dated, and at the crossing the margin is thin by construction. JUDGMENT CALL TO FLAG: this row treats the audited circulation of the issue carrying her essay as the audience for her own work. That is the path the roster note names for her ("a nonfiction author whose audience is built through magazine journalism alongside books"), and it is the only datable 1M for her: no sales figure at or above 1M could be found for any of her books, These Truths (2018) included. An adversarial reading -- that the circulation is the magazine's audience rather than hers -- would push this row to crossing_undatable. a6: 2026 Pulitzer Prize for History, following the p100 Whitehead convention of using the prize year as the scale marker for an author row (https://www.pulitzer.org/prize-winners-by-year/2026). TOOL NOTE: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls across ten concurrent agents) was exhausted during this row; all research from that point used WebFetch, curl and the Wayback CDX API only.

name: Laurent Schwartz
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the IMU's own Fields Medal laureate listing (https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal) names "Laurent Schwartz" under the year heading 1950, alongside Atle Selberg. That is the awarding body's own enumerated table, naming the person. ANNOUNCEMENT YEAR = DESIGNATED YEAR HERE: frame.md requires the announcement year rather than the prize's official designated year. MacTutor states "Harald Bohr presented a Fields Medal to Schwartz at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Harvard on 30 August 1950"; Wikipedia agrees the award was made at the 1950 ICM in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The Fields Medal is announced and conferred at the same congress, so announcement and designation coincide at 1950 and the distinction does not bite on this row. a1: born 5 March 1915 in Paris (MacTutor and Wikipedia agree). a2: doctorate 1943 -- MacTutor: thesis "Etude des sommes d'exponentielles" submitted to the University of Strasbourg in 1943; Wikipedia: the same thesis "published in 1943 ... in the Publications de l'Institut de Mathematique de l'Universite de Clermont-Ferrand". The two institutions are the same one -- Strasbourg was evacuated to Clermont-Ferrand for the war -- so the sources corroborate rather than conflict, and 1943 is the last credential completed. Prior credentials: entered ENS 1934, agregation de mathematiques 1937 (both sources). a3: 1944, the academic year 1944-45 lecturing at the Faculty of Science in Grenoble (MacTutor: "Schwartz spent the academic year 1944-45 lecturing at the Faculty of Science at Grenoble before moving to Nancy"; Wikipedia: "At the end of the war, he spent one year in Grenoble (1944)"). Confidence medium because the wartime years 1940-43 were spent attached to the relocated University of Strasbourg under an assumed name while a doctoral student, and no source found states whether that carried a paid research appointment that would move a3 earlier. a4: RECORDED UNKNOWN DELIBERATELY. His one candidate 'independently created work' is the first publication of the theory of distributions, and the two sources consulted disagree on its year -- MacTutor states the first publication presenting the ideas "appeared in 1948", while the Wikipedia article body gives no date for it at all. Rather than pick one or stretch a bounded range over a disagreement that is not a below-bar/above-bar bracket, this is recorded unknown, matching the other Fields Medal row in the study (p129 Birkar, a4 unknown). a6: unknown, per the standing convention for prize rows with no later distinct scale event. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: not applicable -- non-commercial bucket, no ventures; the criterion is the prize itself and there is no earlier qualifying prize (the Fields Medal was his first, and the 1950 award was only the second round ever held).
